Question: Why is it that the C programming language can be used across multiple different devices but Assembly cannot?
Answer: I assume you mean “multiple different architectures” as opposed to “multiple different devices.” We're long past the days when each computer was unique by about 75 years, give or take. Assembly language isn't one language. Rather, it's the human readable form of the machine code for a particular processor architecture family. Each family has its own instruction set. There may be many different mutually incompatible dialects of assembly code for the same instruction set. For example, look up MASM and AT&T syntax for x86 assembly code. The Z80 is largely backward compatible with the 8080; however, because Intel® copyrighted* their instruction set, Zilog developed their own mnemonics and syntax. (*It’s unclear whether that copyright claim was meaningful.) In fact, you can even have incompatibility within the same assembly language dialect for the same processor family. Newer family members may support instructions and registers that aren't present on older family members, for instance. Instructions for newer processors won't work on older processors that lack those extensions. Now, there have been some assembly translators. It works best when the architectures involved are related, and the newer one takes translation into account. 8080 → 8086 is a famous example. These translators are rare. C code, on the other hand, can be compiled for whatever target architectures the compiler supports. As long as you stick to certain rules and build the right abstractions, it's not that difficult to write portable C code. All you need is a compiler for whatever target architecture you're interested in, and in many cases you are in good shape. It does take effort and care. It's orders of magnitude more approachable than porting large piles of assembly language though. Addendum Since it came up in discussion on a different answer, I figured I would mention it here. If you run the assembled code in a simulator or interpreter, then you can run your assembly language wherever you’ve ported the simulator/interpreter. That assembly language can even target a virtual machine, rather than a real CPU. That particular thread brought up EFI byte code specifically. My answer focuses on assembly code for the native instruction set in its native form. That's what I believe most people think of when they see that phrase without further qualifications. You can develop other kinds of assembly language with different properties. For example, you could create an assembly language that provides a common subset of core operations and abstract “registers,” and use macros or a specialized tool to generate the actual machine code for different machines. Or you could create an assembly language that targets various sorts of virtual machines, such as JVM byte code, CPython byte code, EFI byte code, UCSD pCode, Microsoft’s pCode, etc. When describing it to others, you should call out the fact that it's not traditional native assembly language, otherwise you're likely to cause confusion.

Question: How does UNIX understand that he needs to call tty? How does a tty understand that they want to print to stderr and not stdout?
Answer: How does UNIX understand that he needs to call tty? Who is “he”? Also, TTYs are devices. You can open their device nodes as files. You don't call them like functions. How does a tty understand that they want to print to stderr and not stdout? It doesn't. A TTY device doesn't know anything about stdout or stderr. Those concepts don't exist at its level. The names stdin, stdout, and stderr are the names C gives to the default C file streams set up by the runtime environment prior to entering main(). On a UNIX™ or POSIX system, those three streams are associated with file descriptors 0, 1, and 2. File descriptors are not a C concept, they're a UNIX™/POSIX concept. Other operating systems may use different concepts below file streams. In UNIX™/POSIX, the exec() family of calls replace the current process with a new process for the new program, while retaining a subset of open file descriptors and environment variables. This allows a shell to set up what files it wants associated with file descriptors 0, 1, and 2 before it exec()’s the target program. For an interactive program, all three might be associated with some TTY device such as /dev/tty42 or /dev/ttyS0 or something. Inside a C program, the C runtime library wraps these file descriptors in its FILE* stream abstraction. That's where stdin, stdout, and stderr come in. Those provide a higher level interface, with optional buffering, etc. Typically, stdin and stdout are buffered by default,¹ while stderr isn't.² That buffering is part of the C standard library, and can be reconfigured by your program. Look up setbuf() and setvbuf() for more details. The TTY is oblivious to all this. It just services read and write requests for all the open file descriptors that are associated with it. The division of labor in a UNIX™/POSIX environment is roughly as follows: Now, there's a whole lot more you can dig into with the UNIX™/POSIX terminal interface, and OS-specific APIs and concepts around it. Controlling terminals, cooked/raw, various line disciplines, etc. etc. I’m not going there. I focused on the lowest common denominator: how stdin/stdout/stderr connect a UNIX™/POSIX terminal device. My answer is also specific to UNIX™/POSIX. Other OSes may do things differently. ¹ In fact, the runtime environment could select between line buffered and fully buffered. It might select line buffering for stdin or stdout if detects that it's connected to a TTY. See the UNIX™/POSIX isatty() function. ² At least within C’s FILE* abstraction. Layers outside your program may buffer the data sent to stderr after it leaves your program.

Question: Why is the assembly language dependent on a specific machine or computer?
Answer: Assembly language isn't one language. The exact assembly language details usually do not depend on the exact individual computer you're using. It's not as if each individual computer comes with its own unique assembly language, like a fingerprint. I mention that only because your question could be read that way. The details do depend on: For example, the 8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium, etc. are members of the x86 instruction set architecture family. Later family members introduced extensions to the architecture. The original 8086 is a 16-bit architecture. The 80386 added a 32-bit superset architecture sub-family. AMD™ introduced AMD64, a 64-bit superset that Intel® adapted into highly compatible Intel® 64. Assembly language meant for the 64-bit variant differs from the assembly language for the 32-bit variant. Both differ from the 16-bit variant. The later versions of x86 are (mostly) supersets of the earlier versions: And on top of that there's various extensions such as x87, MMX, multiple generations of SSE, multiple generations of AVX, etc. And that's just one instruction set architecture family. There are many, many others. I’ve personally programmed assembly code for TMS9900, 6502, 8085, 8086, 6805, 8051, TMS320C6000, CP1600, PIC24H, ARMv7, AArch64, and RISC-V (RV64G). I’m certain I have written at least a little code for some other instruction set architectures. Each of those is mutually incompatible with the others. Then there's the assembler tooling. For example, x86 has two major syntax variations: Individual assemblers provide variations on syntax and functionality beyond that, such as different directives and so on.

Question: Why are logic errors more difficult to fix than syntax errors?
Answer: If I, punctuate a; sentence incorrectly it's, pretty obvious especially to native English speakers It's even more; annoying if I forget, to properly terminate—a sentence. That was probably quite painful to read. Your brain picked up on the incorrect syntax right away, long before you had any clue of what I was trying to say. You can spot the errors long before you try to derive any meaning from what I wrote. You can spot the first error just a couple words in. If I told you that “I feel as much like I did yesterday as I do today,” you need to actually try to understand what I wrote before you conclude the sentence as a whole is gibberish. Syntactically, it's just fine. Semantically, it's complete nonsense. That's still a relatively self-contained semantic error. Logic errors include semantic errors such as the one I demonstrated above, as well as larger errors that may span a much larger body of input. For logic errors in software, the error might arise from interactions that span multiple software layers and/or software modules. I recall one weird bug I encountered back in the early days of Linux. The volume sliders for the audio mixer widget went from 0 to 100. The underlying volume registers for the sound card’s hardware mixer went from 0 to 255. The mixer widget looked something like this, although it may not have been GNOME or ALSA at the time. I don't remember which layers contributed directly to the issue, but from what I vaguely remember: a volume setting from user-space wouldn't round-trip correctly from the audio mixer widget to the sound card’s hardware mixer and back. IIRC, writing a new volume and reading it back could return a different, slightly lower volume level. The conversions between the [0,100] range and [0,255] range in both directions apparently truncated a divide result without rounding. In the mixer widget, sliding one channel’s volume slider could cause other channels’ volume levels to drop with each click of the slider. The widget wrote and reread the entire set of mixer settings with each update, and the volume levels ratcheted downward in the process. Oops. That's a logic error that spans the sound card, its driver, the generic sound driver subsystem, the user-space library, and the mixer app. All of those pieces are involved in the volume round-trip, but only one or two of them contributed directly to this error. Happy bug hunting! Also, don't ask me if it was ALSA or OSS, because I don't remember. It was almost 30 years ago. Syntax provides a textual skeleton for you to hang meaning from. In human language, incorrect syntax usually sticks out like a sore thumb. Or, to continue the skeletal analogy, a hyperextended thumb that makes your own thumb ache while you’re looking at it. Semantics govern the meaning itself. If the structure is correct, but the meaning isn't captured correctly, that might be harder to spot. A really subtle semantic error might come across as a vague feeling that “something isn't quite right.” It may not be obvious until you look at things from a different perspective. Continuing the metaphor, consider this upside down face: To most folks, it looks relatively normal, although you might vaguely sense something is off. Now flip it right-side-up: Gahhh! That's still a localized error, but already harder to spot at first. The bigger logic errors happen when multiple entities interact with each other poorly. Everything may seem to make sense locally, but when you put it all together… bam! That's how we end up with instructions like these: Sometimes the error lies in ambiguity and differing interpretations. That's also how we end up with jokes like this: Spouse 1: “Honey, could you pick up a loaf of bread at the store on your way home? And if they have any eggs, please bring home a dozen.” Spouse 2: “Sure, no problem.” Spouse 2 arrives home with a dozen loaves of bread. Spouse 1: “Why did you buy a dozen loaves of bread?!?” Spouse 2: “The store had eggs!” *d’oh* These principles hold whether you're trying to communicate with another person or with a computer. The more you need to take into account and understand to see the error, the harder it will be to find. And if the error arises arises from differing interpretations of the same input, it may need a second set of eyes or a change in perspective to spot it.

Question: Is it possible that CPU and other types of caches may become obsolete with increased data transfer speeds?
Answer: Don’t confuse bandwidth with latency. Minimum latency to system RAM hasn’t really budged in a long time, even though transfer rates continue to increase. You can access a CPU register in a modern CPU in a fraction of a nanosecond. You can access data in L1 cache in around a nanosecond, and L2 may only be a few nanoseconds further away.* System memory accesses, on the other hand, take anywhere from dozens to hundreds of nanoseconds. Those latencies are measured from when you request the data until the first chunk of data arrives. Bandwidth describes how long it takes to move a block of data. If you request a block of data in an otherwise-idle memory system, increasing the bandwidth with reduce the amount of time from the first chunk of data to the last. Most CPU loads and stores ask for a single chunk of data, however. Streaming workloads, such as you find in traditional GPU applications, care way more about bandwidth than latency. They’re moving large quantities of data and have a ton of work in flight. The work itself is divided up into a large number of independent streams. Each of those streams runs concurrently, sopping up the available bandwidth. Overall throughput then bottlenecks on memory bandwidth, even if individual streams experience gaps in execution due to memory system latency. General purpose computing cares quite a bit about latency as well. Pointer-chasing workloads are particularly sensitive to latency. If you need to dereference a pointer to get the data, you’re stuck waiting for the data before you can operate on it. If you’re chasing a linked list or tree, each iteration can go no faster than p = p->next or p = p->child. Higher bandwidth does typically reduce the average latency on a heavily loaded processor. In practice, it doesn’t really affect the baseline latency that much, however. DDR5’s baseline latency is similar to DDR4’s, for example. That baseline is much higher than what you see in an L1 or L2 cache. You’re limited by the physics of getting data from waaaaaay over there and up into the processor. The speed of light sets a lower bound, but many other factors (capacitance, inductance, switching speeds, etc) raise the lower bound even higher. *For instance, consider a 4GHz processor with single-cycle register access, a 4 cycle load-to-use latency to L1, and 12 cycle load-to-use latency to L2. Register access takes 0.25ns, L1 takes 1ns, and L2 takes 3ns. That’s roughly in line with an AMD Zen 3 processor at 4GHz.

Question: Why don't more programmers use regular expressions? Somehow, most of the programmers I know prefer to use split/substring with index, etc.
Answer: There are a solid handful of good answers here that deserve your attention. In no particular order, I suggest reading each of these: I won't repeat the “now you have two problems” joke from Jamie Zawinski (aka jwz). I suspect he might be tired of it. [See: https://www.jwz.org/blog/2014/05/so-this-happened/] Instead, pun dog to the rescue. I share this as a self-aware fan of Perl, BTW: As the other answers I linked point out, regular expressions are: I generally agree with all of those points. In their classic form, regexes are essentially machine code for a certain category of finite state machines. They just happen to use opcodes that map to punctuation so that it's possible to get by without an assembler. ;-) OK, that's not literally true. Still, it's a sufficiently useful metaphor to capture the essence. I give my own take below. I will try not to retread too much ground already covered in the answers I linked. Please, go read them! I’m here to recount my own experience. Regexes On The Fly One place I absolutely love using regular expressions is in my text editor (Vim) and with the classic UNIX™ utility grep and its younger cousin egrep (“extended grep”).¹ In both of those use cases, I am writing a regular expression on the fly for a specific, immediate, and transient need. Readability? Maintainability? Who cares?!? Those regular expressions won't persist in any codebase, other than a few that I keep in my .vimrc. They just need to work in the moment. After that, they're gone. There's no consequence to getting one wrong, either. Just hit undo (if necessary) and try again! What about in some software’s codebase? Perl: Regexes as a Lifestyle Perl took awk, sed, grep, C, and a dash of sh (Bourne shell), and munged them all together into one language.² Regular expressions are a first class feature of the language. You would be forgiven for thinking it’s a regular expression engine with a scripting language just sorta tacked onto it. That prints all lines from stdin that look roughly like assignment statements. And, the fact I had to explain that hints why regular expressions are not so great in codebases: They quickly become difficult to follow. That one actually isn't all that bad. But, it still, it's wrapped a lot of work up in a 30-character string. When writing Perl, I do as Perl programmers do and let regexes flow. I set a low bar for when to apply a regular expression, as the language really does make it easy. Too easy, perhaps. I avoid complicated back references and conditionals and most of the fancy features. I don't need them often. When I do, I have two choices: Usually the latter wins. After all, if I write at the limit of my cleverness, it's probably beyond my ability to debug. And anyone else that maintains the code is going to be cursing my name. That's not to say I haven't used such beasts. I have at least one program that uses a gnarly regex I found in a cookbook, already debugged. I used it like a black box. In many Perl programs, regular expressions often run afoul of the old saying “If the only tool you have is a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.” Regexes aren't the only tool Perl has, by far. Perl’s regex hammer is really darn shiny, though. It's also comfortable, capable, and nearly always near the top of the toolbox. When you pick it up, its handle is usually still warm from the last time you held it. I focused on Perl so heavily in my answer so far because it's the only language I’ve programmed where I consistently ended up preferring regular expressions over other, more focused constructs. For example, I spotted code similar to this in one of my old scripts: Did that really call for a regex? It feels natural to me in Perl, and unnatural in nearly any other language I use. Elsewhere, I would just compare against the two strings with an ordinary comparison. Other Languages The only other language I made heavy use of regexes in was Lex and its cousin Flex. Programs in those languages specify match patterns and actions for lexical scanners. Lex and Flex use regular expressions to match lexical elements in the input stream. In Lex, a pattern match and associated action might look like this: Other than that, I don't use regular expressions very often at all. There's nearly always a better option. And by “better,” I mean clearer, more focused, and often more efficient option. C++ has added std::regex to its standard library. While I was happy to see it added, I have actually only used it twice, I think, and I can only really remember one major use of it that I will get to at the end. These days, if I have a task that needs a lot of parsing, I will often just reach for a parser generator. Or, if a parser already exists for the input language, I will just grab that instead. If I do use a parser generator, any regexes I write will live in the lexical scanner. The rest of the code doesn't need them. I’ve read a number of stories about regexes blowing up in production. Certain features can result in quadratic or exponential explosion in runtime on adversarial inputs. Many input languages aren't regular, and therefore can't be parsed properly by regular expressions.³ [X]HTML in particular is not a regular language, as this classic Stack Overflow answer reminds us: https://stackoverflow.com/a/1732454  My Favorite (Ab)use of std::regex in C++ Two $DAYJOBs back, I wrote a constraint-solver based tool for generating assembly language test cases to verify a CPU design. The input language looks similar to assembly language, but with details missing. The tool then fills in the missing details by randomly selecting from whatever options remain after applying the constraints. For example, suppose I want an ADD instruction that feeds another ADD instruction. I could write the constraint “ADD => ADD” and the tool would figure out the rest, including allocating and initializing registers, adding code to check results, etc. The => says “The instruction on the right must consume a value produced by the instruction on the left.” In contrast, -> just means “These instructions must appear in sequence.” You could also be more explicit about the connections between instructions by using variables. Suppose I want to add and subtract the same two inputs, and then multiply those together. In this example, I don't really care where they came from either, as long as it came from two other randomly selected instructions rather than constants supplied by the tool: The . means “any instruction”,⁴ while .. in the argument list means “unspecified arguments”. I ran into a design issue: Sometimes I want to specify a subset of the instruction set based on a detail that isn't represented by one of the syntax elements available to me in the pseudo-assembly syntax. For instance, we didn't have separate register files for integer and floating point, so I couldn't use a register constraint to force selecting a floating point instruction. And that's where regular expressions parachuted in to the rescue. Our instruction set mnemonics used a set of very useful naming conventions: I added a feature where you could specify an instruction mnemonic constraint with an extended regular expression. In place of a mnemonic, you’d put a regular expression in-between slashes. The user-supplied regex was then used to filter the mnemonic list. For example, suppose I want to test scalar single precision floating point instructions on values read from memory: That picks instructions whose mnemonic doesn't start with V, thus excluding vector instructions, but does end in SP, thereby giving me all the relevant 3-operand single precision floating point instructions. Or, suppose I wanted to test the shift and rotate instructions, but only on byte operands. This will generate those, and the tool takes care of the rest: That would match SHRB, SHRUB, SHLB, ROTLB, ROTRB, and their vector cousins VSHRB, VSHRUB, VSHLB, VROTLB, VROTLB. Want to test all the multiplies? /MPY/ does the trick, even if we add or remove some multiplies from the instruction set definition. If you want to get dot products into the mix, do /(MPY|DOTP)/. Want a generic move instruction that's agnostic about its arguments? That'll match MV, MVC, VMVK, MVK49, MVK64, etc. etc. Occasionally a regex might allow an unintended instruction; however, I didn't see that as a huge problem. We were generating large numbers of tests, and so the few instructions that snuck through would just get a little extra testing, while the instructions they displaced would get slightly less. Was there a better way? It depends on what you mean by better. This was primarily a one person project, and I had a lot of bigger fish to fry in its construction. My customers were already familiar with Perl and regex, as much of our infrastructure was built on Perl. I could have designed more focused instruction selection functionality. It would have taken more time and more code, and would have been less flexible. OTOH, taking a regex from the user and feeding it to std::regex took less than a day. Had I stayed longer at that job, I probably would have added other, more focused mechanisms for filtering the instruction list. I would probably also retain the regex feature as an escape valve, because it was just so effective! So, I think I made the right tradeoff given the position I was in. I couldn't anticipate all the ways it might be used, but I could see it could be very general, powerful, and flexible. Punchline Regexes are cool and powerful, but best used sparingly—if at all—in most code. Sometimes they're exactly the right tool for the job. Usually there are better, more focused tools available. Go nuts with them in your editor though. ¹ Back in the day, I also used fgrep (“fixed grep”), although modern implementations have made fgrep and even egrep unnecessary. grep -F and grep -E correspond to fgrep and egrep, respectively. egrep is still shorter to type than grep -E, and modern implementations of grep optimize fixed string searches automatically. ² The result was far better than Fish Pork-a-roni a’la Simpson, in my opinion. However, there are plenty of folks that, like Bart, would rather not have nuggified fish porklets. Reference: ³ Although they might be tokenized just fine by a regex based lexer. You may need start conditions to make some of the match patterns context dependent. ⁴ Well, not exactly, but it's close enough for this answer.

Question: Is using statement expressions considered bad practice? If not, for what reason is it not in the C Standard?
Answer: It depends on what you mean by “statement expression.” If you’re referring to the GNU compiler extension, see the second half of this answer. C11 Standard In the C11 standard, footnote 84 refers to statement expressions in a way that clearly means expression statements, suggesting the terms might be interchangeable: 84) This paragraph renders undefined statement expressions such as while allowing Link: https://port70.net/~nsz/c/c11/n1570.html#note84 In C, most statements are expression statements. That puts() call is an expression statement. Section 6.8.3 of the C11 standard defines expression statements and null statements. An expression statement is literally just an expression followed by a semicolon. A null statement omits the expression. Grammatically, both fall under the production expression-statement in the grammar. expression-statement : expression o p t   ; Link: https://port70.net/~nsz/c/c11/n1570.html#6.8.3 GNU Extension Now, you may be referring to the GNU extension that allows wrapping a compound statement in parentheses to return a value, like this: Link: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Statement-Exprs.html I’m personally not a fan, and I’ve been able to avoid writing statement statement expressions myself in the code I write. Nearly all potential uses of GNU statement expressions are better served by a static inline function in my estimation. That said, nearly all isn’t all. Statement expressions have access to the local variable context that a static inline function does not. While you might consider that a feature, it’s a trap for maintenance programmers down the line. Direct access to local variables that aren’t explicit arguments—or write access to local variables that are explicit arguments—tends to catch people off guard. That macro that looks like a function call can fiddle things you don’t expect a function call to fiddle. Statement expressions can also provide a form of polymorphism. That’s somewhat more compelling. I’ve worked with codebases that make use of them to implement type-checked polymorphic primitives in C, such as these from ARM’s Trusted Firmware reference code: If I try to call MIN() with an int and a uint32_t, that’s a compile error rather than a surprise loss of signed-ness. Granted, other warnings normally would catch the mixed signs; this just makes it even harder to ignore. These macros enforce type safety using other compiler magic. In for a penny, in for a pound, I suppose. That suggests statement expressions are most useful when you bring in a handful of other features, as the example above illustrates. With that in mind, I would leave this sort of magic to library authors by default. I would avoid it in portable code.

Question: Why were CGA and EGA digital, but VGA analogue?
Answer: It comes down to a combination of color gamut and video bandwidth. As Phillip Remaker’s answer rightly points out, bandwidth is a major issue. I do have a quibble with his answer, however. CGA, EGA, and VGA all place limits on the number of colors you can display simultaneously. However, that doesn’t affect what goes over the cable. Rather, the gamut of possible colors affects what goes over the cable. And as Phillip rightly pointed out, the pixel clock kept increasing as well. The real story emerges when you multiply the bits per pixel by the pixel clock. When you go from CGA to EGA, the bandwidth nearly doubles: ~58Mbps to ~98Mbps. That’s not to bad to absorb at that time. When you go from EGA to VGA, the bandwidth increases by a factor of 4.5 to ~453Mbps. Yowzers! That’s maybe a bit much for 1987 technology. To send that data digitally would require a firehose of a cable and a correspondingly chonky connector also, since it would likely be sent as parallel data rather than serial. Going to analog also enabled third parties to push the pixel clock and resolution further more easily. And by easily, I primarily mean cost effectively. Analog remained the most cost effective way to send high bandwidth video in PCs until digital technology caught up at a price point that enabled wide-scale deployment. Echoing CGA’s origins, that happened around the time television went digital. PC displays and TVs started out joined at the hip, and have ended up joined at the hip once again.

Question: Why was UNIX designed such that a parent process cannot directly call exec() without first having to call fork() and thereby copying (or using COW semantics for) all of the parent’s data structures which are seldom used by the child process anyway?
Answer: Who says you can’t directly call exec() without calling fork() first? Sure, it will replace the current process with the new process, but sometimes that’s exactly what you want. It happens often enough that the Bourne shell includes an exec command which does exactly that. That feature allows you to write programs that are wrappers around other programs. These wrappers can configure and/or edit the environment before exec’ing the target, such as: For example, suppose I have some fiddly proprietary software, let’s call it CrankySoft™, that requires its utility binaries to be in the $PATH. But, I have two versions of CrankySoft™ installed, one for legacy projects and one for new projects, and both have identically named utility binaries. Even worse, both also need to dynamically load shared libraries specific to the CrankySoft™ version that are also identically named. I can make wrapper shell scripts cranky-1.0 and cranky-2.0 to handle this. Perhaps something like this would do for cranky-1.0: And the script for cranky-2.0 might look similar, with v1.0 changed to v2.0 in the paths. Lest you think I’m making this scenario up out of whole cloth, I’ve had this sort of thing come up many times in my career. The exec statement at the end of the script calls exec() directly without fork(), replacing the shell interpreting the script with the executable. There’s no reason to keep the shell interpreter around once we’ve launched CrankySoft™. The wrapper might also be written in C, C++, or other language. They’ll rely on POSIX C APIs for this—or the system calls behind them—so I’ll focus on C. I’ve written security wrappers in C that wipe out all but the most essential UNIX™ environment variables, strip nearly all command line arguments, close all file descriptors, and then connect stdin/stdout/stderr to /dev/null or other explicit location before calling exec() on a security-sensitive executable. From C code, you can make all the environment modifications I mentioned above, as well as a few more,* such as: The UNIX™ nohup command is an example of that first bullet: It masks SIGHUP before exec()’ing the target program. The nice, chrt, and taskset commands are examples of the second bullet. I believe taskset is Linux-specific. The su and chgrp commands change user/group ID before exec()’ing a target command or shell. The chroot command uses the chroot() API to change the effective root directory before exec()’ing the target. (*It’s possible some shells can do some or all of these as well.) You might be thinking “OK, so? That still doesn’t answer why I should fork() then exec() for more typical applications.” Well, it kinda does, at least for one set of use cases. Often, you’ll want to redirect some combination of stdin, stdout, and stderr before launching a particular program. You might want to open or close other file descriptors*. You might also want to tweak an environment variable or three without duplicating the whole environment to use with execve(). You might want to setuid()/setgid() to a different user, particularly if you’re a daemon like sshd or httpd. (*Yes, I’m aware of close-on-exec, but that’s a recent flag in the history of UNIX™. It was added to POSIX in 2008.) And, of course, you can call fork() without calling exec(). The parent and child processes get separate virtual address spaces. But, they still share file descriptors, and so they can still communicate with each other. When fork() and exec() are separate steps, you can perform arbitrary amounts of work in the child before calling exec() without affecting the parent. That also lets you do other interesting things, such as setting up process and thread pools. Now let me preface this next example with the caveat that I haven’t dug into webserver technology and configuration in many years. The example may be out of date—I don’t know if it is!—but that doesn’t invalidate it. Some webservers such as Apache let you set up a worker pool, potentially with multiple child processes to manage all the workers. Apache can pre-fork() multiple child processes. Each child process manages some number of worker threads each. The parent process holds onto root permissions so it can bind ports 80 and 443, while dropping permissions in the child processes. The child processes each manage some number of worker threads. The child processes handle restarting worker threads if any worker dies. And the parent process can handle restarting a child process if any child dies. And, child processes can voluntarily terminate after some number of requests as a hedge against memory leaks and heap fragmentation. That encapsulation makes the webserver more robust against bugs in the server itself, as well as transient issues such as a brief out-of-memory situation that causes one of the workers to crash. OOM is less a big deal today, but it was a much bigger deal back in the day. And, back in the day, Common Gateway Interface (CGI) was all the rage. CGI gives you a way to invoke an external program to satisfy a request for a particular URL. The webserver heavily curates the environment seen by that program—like the wrapper example above—and passes details of the request on stdin. The CGI program then outputs the content to send to the client on stdout. Again, this is a case where the parent thread/process needs to curate the view of the world for the child after fork(), but before calling exec(). In Apache’s case, it could even launch a separate process to handle CGI requests, so that a fork() wouldn’t require cloning a bunch of worker threads. The CGI daemon communicates with the other worker threads through a socket. You also mentioned the cost of copying the parent and/or using COW. Copying the parent is indeed expensive! That’s what lead to the invention of vfork(). vfork() doesn’t split the child process’ virtual address space from the parent. Rather, it trusts that the only thing you’re going to do after vfork() is call exec() or _exit() (presumably when exec() fails). For the extremely common case of calling fork() and then immediately calling exec(), vfork() can speed things up on systems that actually need to copy some or all of the parent process context on a fork(). But, vfork() is a fragile hack. Thankfully, COW is now the norm, and modern OSes have optimized fork() quite a bit. For programs that call fork() followed immediately by exec(), very few writable data pages will get COW’d in the child. The main remaining cost involves copying the page tables for the child. If the OS can manage to COW those, that should reduce the cost of fork() in a process with a larger virtual address space. For some reason, I thought Linux already did this; however, I might just be remembering discussions from many years ago that don’t actually represent what Linux implements. This LWN link shows that the idea was under active discussion a year and a half ago: Link: https://lwn.net/ml/linux-kernel/20220519183127.3909598-1-shiyn.lin@gmail.com/ From one of the messages in the thread: The paper mentioned a list of benchmarks of the time cost for On-Demand fork. For example, on Redis, the meantime of fork when taking the snapshot. Default fork() got 7.40 ms; On-demand Fork (COW PTE table) got 0.12 ms. So, yes, there are still some optimizations we can perform. Circling back around to why: The UNIX™ philosophy is to provide many sharply focused tools that are effective at what they do, and can be composed with each other easily to create higher-order operations. fork() and exec() are no exceptions here. Hopefully my examples above show how that separation can be beneficial.

Question: What is the convention of the header files name in C++, using .h or .hpp?
Answer: There isn't one convention for C++. I have personally seen or read about the conventions below for C++ implementation and header files. I list implementation file extension followed by header file extension. Convention #1 above doesn't work unless you have a case preserving filesystem, and ideally a case sensitive file system. It’s an ancient convention that everyone has long abandoned. I don't recommend it to anyone. Convention #2 is quite common. I think I first encountered it in Turbo C++. The acronym “cpp” irks me a bit, however, as it feels MS-DOS-ish and it's traditionally the name of the C preprocessor. It also leads to folks calling the language CPP, which is even worse. But with CppCon and CppReference, I’m overruled I guess. 😋 Convention #3 seems pretty rare in my personal experience. The xs read like wildcards to me, similar to .c?? and .h??. I think they're supposed to be rotated + signs. Meh. Convention #4 is the Google coding style. If I could change one superficial thing in the Google C++ style, it would be to give C++-only headers a different extension from C compatible extensions. I am no longer bound by Google’s C++ style guide, so ¯⁠\⁠_⁠(⁠ツ⁠)⁠_⁠/⁠¯. Convention #5 is my current favorite. Concise and easy to type. Nice symmetry, and no aliasing with other tools. It escapes the DOS world’s tendency to bloat extensions to 3 characters as well. EDIT: in the comments, Tim Muston and Keith Thompson mentioned they’ve seen .cpp / .h. I believe I’ve used that at one point as well. Which convention should you use? For your own projects, use whichever one you like.* Just be sure to be consistent. If your development environment is already set up to favor a particular convention, you might let it make the decision for you. (*Except #1 above. It will almost certainly end in sadness.) If you’re contributing to another project, follow its style for your contributions. Likewise, if your employer has a particular style, use theirs for the code you write for them. I make some additional common sense suggestions in this related answer I wrote a couple years ago: And for goodness sakes: keep all the filenames lowercase for maximum portability among systems, and refer to them by lowercase names in #include directives. Also, use forward slashes for path separators in #include directives as well, even on Windows. Every C and C++ compiler I’ve used there translates forward slashes silently if needed, but none have translated backslashes. Also, backslashes need to be escaped and forward slashes don't. Sure, there are still some shouty DOS like systems around here or there, but typically the C and C++ compilers on those platforms handle lowercase in #include just fine. And it's pretty easy to force filenames to lowercase when bringing them to modern systems. I mention this because it's a real world problem. I once had to deal with moving a fairly large DSP software project developed under Windows to *nix. Someone decided to be cute and use CamelCase on some filenames, but not consistently everywhere. They also had a thing for backslashes in #include directives. I ended up using a Perl script to lowercase all #include directives and filenames before proceeding. I also had it find and fix the #include “foo\\bar.h” crap that showed up here and there. Once I was done, the code compiled equally well in *nix and Windows. (Well, cross compiled at least, since it was for our DSPs.)

Question: Why would a question asked 6 months ago suddenly appear yesterday?
Answer: Quora routinely cycles old content into people's feeds. For example, I didn't have to scroll very far to find this in my feed: From what I have noticed, it's usually older answers that show up from time to time. However, I suspect these “greatest hits” answers sometimes trigger others to write their own new answers to the same question. Quora is driven by engagement. If an old question starts stirring up engagement, I’d guess Quora pulls it out of mothballs and starts feeding the question itself to more folks. That's not just an idle guess. Recently, I saw several answers to a question from over a year ago. That question asked about inflation, right around the time inflation had peaked and was starting to decline in the US. Answer: Who would you be if you had different parents? There's only a bit under 8 billion living examples to choose from. Without any other constraints, this question isn't particularly meaningful. I believe the other answers have invented some constraints to make it tractable. Otherwise, you end up with languages as diverse as Python, INTERCAL, MUMPS, Object Oriented COBOL, and so on. A more interesting question might be: What aspects of C++ would you change if you didn't need to be highly compatible with C? Some ideas off the top of my head: And lots of other stuff. But guess what? Languages that already do these sorts of things and more exist. Pick one that's as C++-like as you wish, and you have your answer. Java? C#? Something else?
